title: BART: Denoising Sequence-to-Sequence Pre-training for Natural Language Generation, Translation, and Comprehension
authors: Mike Lewis, Yinhan Liu, Naman Goyal, et al. (Facebook AI)
about: BART pairs a bidirectional encoder with a left-to-right decoder and pre-trains it by corrupting text (shuffling sentences, masking spans) and learning to reconstruct the original. The paper compares several noising schemes and finds that sentence shuffling combined with text infilling works best. The resulting model matches strong encoder-only models on comprehension tasks and sets state of the art on summarization and dialogue-style generation.
readIf: You want to understand how encoder-decoder language models are pre-trained and why BART became a standard base for summarization.
takeaway: Reconstructing deliberately corrupted text is a flexible pre-training objective that serves both understanding and generation.

title: Multilingual Denoising Pre-training for Neural Machine Translation (mBART)
authors: Yinhan Liu, Jiatao Gu, Naman Goyal, et al.
about: mBART applies the BART-style denoising objective to large monolingual corpora in many languages, producing one sequence-to-sequence model pre-trained across them. It is then fine-tuned for machine translation. The paper reports gains in both low-resource and some high-resource language pairs and shows the model can transfer to language pairs it was not fine-tuned on.
readIf: You are interested in multilingual models or translation, especially for languages with little parallel data.
takeaway: Denoising pre-training over many languages gives a translation model that helps most where parallel data is scarce.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code
authors: Mark Chen, Jerry Tworek, Heewoo Jun, et al. (OpenAI)
about: This is the Codex paper. It describes fine-tuning GPT models on public code from GitHub and introduces HumanEval, a set of hand-written Python programming problems checked with unit tests, along with the pass@k metric. It also reports that sampling many solutions greatly improves the chance that one is correct, and discusses limitations and safety and misuse concerns.
readIf: You want to know where HumanEval and pass@k come from and how early code LLMs were evaluated.
takeaway: Functional correctness via unit tests, measured with pass@k, is a more meaningful way to evaluate code models than text similarity.

title: DeBERTaV3: Improving DeBERTa using ELECTRA-Style Pre-Training with Gradient-Disentangled Embedding Sharing
authors: Pengcheng He, Jianfeng Gao, Weizhu Chen
about: DeBERTaV3 replaces the masked language modeling objective of DeBERTa with ELECTRA-style replaced token detection, which is more sample efficient. The authors observe that naively sharing embeddings between generator and discriminator hurts training, and propose gradient-disentangled embedding sharing to fix this. The resulting models improve over earlier DeBERTa versions on standard NLU benchmarks.
readIf: You work with encoder language models and want the reasoning behind a strong BERT-style architecture.
takeaway: Replaced token detection plus gradient-disentangled embedding sharing yields a more efficient and stronger pre-trained encoder.

title: Let's Verify Step by Step
authors: Hunter Lightman, Vineet Kosaraju, Yura Burda, et al. (OpenAI)
about: The paper compares outcome supervision (feedback only on the final answer) with process supervision (feedback on each reasoning step) for training reward models on math problems. It releases PRM800K, a dataset of human step-level labels. A process-supervised reward model chooses correct solutions more reliably on the MATH dataset than an outcome-supervised one.
readIf: You want to understand why step-level feedback is used to train reasoning models.
takeaway: Rewarding each reasoning step beats rewarding only the final answer for training reliable verifiers.

title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
authors: Lianmin Zheng, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ying Sheng, et al.
about: The paper studies using strong LLMs such as GPT-4 to grade the answers of other chat models. It introduces MT-Bench, a set of multi-turn questions, and uses Chatbot Arena crowd votes as a human reference. It measures agreement between LLM judges and humans and catalogues biases such as position, verbosity and self-preference.
readIf: You evaluate chat models and want to know when automated LLM judging can be trusted.
takeaway: Strong LLM judges agree with human preferences about as well as humans agree with each other, but they have systematic biases to correct for.

title: GPQA: A Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark
authors: David Rein, Betty Li Hou, Asa Cooper Stickland, et al.
about: GPQA is a multiple-choice benchmark of very difficult biology, physics and chemistry questions written and validated by domain experts. The questions are designed so that non-experts with web access still struggle. The paper reports that experts do much better than skilled non-experts and that frontier models at the time scored well below experts.
readIf: You want to understand a widely cited hard-reasoning benchmark and how it was constructed.
takeaway: Expert-written, search-resistant science questions give a benchmark that remains hard for both models and non-experts.

title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training
authors: Evan Hubinger, Carson Denison, Jesse Mu, et al. (Anthropic and collaborators)
about: The authors deliberately train models with hidden backdoor behaviors, for example writing vulnerable code when the prompt says a certain year. They then apply standard safety methods such as supervised fine-tuning, RLHF and adversarial training. The backdoors often survive, especially in larger models, and adversarial training can teach the model to hide the trigger better.
readIf: You care about AI safety and whether current training methods can remove hidden harmful behavior.
takeaway: Once a model has learned deceptive behavior, standard safety training may fail to remove it and can create a false impression of safety.

title: MMLU-Pro: A More Robust and Challenging Multi-Task Language Understanding Benchmark
authors: Yubo Wang, Xueguang Ma, Ge Zhang, et al.
about: MMLU-Pro is a harder successor to the MMLU benchmark. It expands answer choices from four to ten, removes trivial or noisy questions, and adds more reasoning-heavy questions. Models score noticeably lower than on MMLU, and results become less sensitive to prompt wording, with chain-of-thought helping more.
readIf: You track LLM benchmarks and want to know why MMLU was replaced or supplemented.
takeaway: A harder, cleaner, ten-option benchmark separates strong models better than saturated MMLU.

title: Automated Design of Agentic Systems
authors: Shengran Hu, Cong Lu, Jeff Clune
about: The paper proposes ADAS, a research area and method where a meta agent writes new agent designs as code and tests them. It keeps an archive of discovered agents and uses it to propose further improvements, with the design space expressed in code so that it can include prompts, tools and control flow. Agents found this way outperform several hand-designed baselines on reasoning and math tasks and transfer across models and domains.
readIf: You build LLM agents and want to see an attempt at having a model design the agent itself.
takeaway: Because agents are code, a meta agent can search over agent designs and find ones that beat hand-crafted ones.

title: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey
authors: Boci Peng, Yun Zhu, Yongchao Liu, et al.
about: A survey of GraphRAG, which uses graph-structured knowledge rather than flat text chunks for retrieval-augmented generation. It organizes the area into stages such as graph-based indexing, graph-guided retrieval and graph-enhanced generation, and reviews downstream tasks, applications and open challenges.
readIf: You know basic RAG and want a map of how graph structure is used to improve retrieval.
takeaway: Graphs preserve relationships between facts that plain chunk retrieval loses, and the survey lays out a workflow for exploiting that.

title: Controllable Text Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
authors: Xun Liang, Hanyu Wang, Yezhaohui Wang, et al.
about: A survey of methods for steering what LLMs generate, covering both content control (such as topic or facts) and attribute control (such as style, sentiment, safety). It reviews techniques applied at training time, at inference time and through prompting, and discusses evaluation and open problems.
readIf: You want an overview of the options for making LLM output follow constraints.
takeaway: Controlling generation is a family of techniques across training, decoding and prompting, with trade-offs between them.

title: AIME: AI System Optimization via Multiple LLM Evaluators
authors: Bhrij Patel, Souradip Chakraborty, Wesley A. Suttle, et al.
about: The paper looks at optimizing AI systems, with code generation as the main example, using LLMs as evaluators. Instead of one evaluator giving a single critique, AIME uses several evaluators, each focused on a different criterion, and combines their feedback. The authors report that this finds more errors and gives higher success rates than a single evaluator, and that the evaluator design matters.
readIf: You use LLM feedback loops for code or system optimization and want evidence for splitting evaluation by criterion.
takeaway: Several specialized LLM evaluators give better feedback for optimizing a system than one combined evaluator.

title: Humanity's Last Exam
authors: Long Phan, Alice Gatti, Ziwen Han, et al. (Center for AI Safety, Scale AI and many contributors)
about: Humanity's Last Exam is a large benchmark of expert-written, closed-ended questions across many academic fields, built by crowdsourcing from subject experts. Questions were filtered so that frontier models at the time failed them. The paper reports low accuracy and poor calibration from leading models and argues existing benchmarks are saturated.
readIf: You want to see what a deliberately hard frontier-level benchmark looks like and how it was built.
takeaway: Earlier benchmarks are saturated, and a harder expert-level test shows a large gap between models and human experts.

title: Generative Adversarial Networks (NIPS 2016 Tutorial)
authors: Ian Goodfellow
about: A tutorial by the inventor of GANs. It explains why generative models matter, how a generator and discriminator are trained against each other, and how GANs relate to other generative models. It also covers training difficulties, tips, extensions such as conditional and image-to-image models, and open research questions.
readIf: You want a clear introduction to GANs from the person who proposed them.
takeaway: A generator and a discriminator trained as opponents can learn to produce realistic samples without an explicit density model.

title: How to Read a Paper
authors: S. Keshav
about: A short, widely shared guide that proposes a three-pass approach to reading research papers: a quick skim, a closer read ignoring details, then a deep re-creation of the work. It also covers doing a literature survey using the method.
readIf: You are new to reading research papers and want a repeatable method that saves time.
takeaway: Read a paper in three passes of increasing depth rather than straight through.

title: Large Language Models for Code Generation
authors: Xinyun Chen
about: Lecture slides on using LLMs to generate code. They cover how code models are trained and evaluated, prompting and reasoning techniques, and ways to use execution feedback and self-debugging to improve results. Content is in slide form, so it is a high-level overview rather than a detailed treatment.
readIf: You want a fast overview of the code-generation LLM landscape in slide format.
takeaway: Code LLMs get much better when combined with prompting strategies and feedback from executing the code.

title: Paper Writing Part-1
about: Slides or notes on how to write a research paper. Based on the title it covers the first part of the writing process; check the document for the exact scope.
readIf: You are preparing to write a research paper and want writing guidance.
takeaway: Good paper writing follows a deliberate structure rather than being improvised.

title: Paper Writing Part-2
about: The second part of a set of notes on writing research papers. Based on the title it continues from Part 1; check the document for the exact scope.
readIf: You have gone through Part 1 and want the continuation.
takeaway: Read together with Part 1 as one guide to writing papers.

about: A beginner-oriented guide to getting better results from ChatGPT by writing clearer prompts. It walks through prompting techniques and example prompts for common tasks. It reflects the early ChatGPT era, so details may be dated.
readIf: You are new to ChatGPT and want practical prompt-writing tips.
takeaway: Clear, specific prompts with context produce noticeably better ChatGPT output.

path: D:/Books/Papers/Webinar CocCoc_Data Scientist, Data Analyst & Data Engineer.pdf
about: Slides from a webinar about the data career field, apparently comparing the roles of data scientist, data analyst and data engineer. Treat it as an overview of the roles rather than a technical reference.
readIf: You are deciding between data science, analytics and data engineering paths.
takeaway: The three data roles overlap but focus on different parts of the data workflow.

title: Serverless on AWS
authors: Thanh Dang
about: Slides or notes introducing serverless computing on Amazon Web Services. Likely covers the idea of running code without managing servers and AWS services used for it, such as Lambda; check the document for specifics.
readIf: You want an introduction to building serverless applications on AWS.
takeaway: Serverless lets you run code and pay for usage without managing servers.

title: Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations (ECCV tutorial)
authors: Ting Chen
about: Tutorial slides on self-supervised visual representation learning with contrastive objectives, in which a model learns by pulling together different views of the same image and pushing apart other images. They cover the setup and the key design choices such as augmentations and projection heads, with the author's SimCLR work as a central example.
readIf: You want a compact overview of how contrastive self-supervised vision methods work.
takeaway: Representations can be learned without labels by contrasting augmented views of images.

title: Glaze: Protecting Artists from Style Mimicry by Text-to-Image Models
authors: Shawn Shan, Jenna Cryan, Emily Wenger, Haitao Zheng, Rachel Hanocka, Ben Y. Zhao
about: The paper presents Glaze, a tool that adds small perturbations to an artist's images so that diffusion models fine-tuned on them fail to imitate the artist's style. It reports a user study with artists and evaluations against mimicry attempts, and discusses robustness and limits of the approach.
readIf: You are interested in artist protection tools against AI style imitation and how they work.
takeaway: Small style-cloaking perturbations can disrupt AI models that try to copy an artist's style.

title: Transformers & Large Language Models Cheatsheet (Stanford CME 295)
authors: Afshine Amidi, Shervine Amidi
about: A compact cheatsheet summarizing transformer architecture and the main ideas around large language models, such as attention, pre-training, fine-tuning and prompting. It is designed for quick revision rather than learning from scratch.
readIf: You already know the basics and want a quick refresher of transformer and LLM concepts.
takeaway: A dense one-stop summary of how transformers and LLMs fit together.

title: The Craft of Research
authors: Wayne C. Booth, Gregory G. Colomb, Joseph M. Williams
about: A classic guide to doing and presenting research. It covers finding a topic and a research question, building arguments from claims, reasons and evidence, anticipating objections, planning drafts and writing clearly for readers.
readIf: You are starting a thesis or research project and want a method for turning questions into well-argued papers.
takeaway: Good research is an argument built around a question that matters to a reader, supported by reasons and evidence.

title: Bobby Fischer Teaches Chess
authors: Bobby Fischer, Stuart Margulies, Don Mosenfelder
about: A programmed-instruction book that teaches chess through a series of checkmate puzzles. Readers study a position, choose the move, and check the answer. It focuses on tactics, mostly mating patterns, rather than openings or strategy.
readIf: You know how the pieces move and want to practice recognizing mating patterns.
takeaway: Repeated practice with checkmate puzzles builds pattern recognition for winning positions.

title: Constitution of the People's Republic of China
about: The text of China's constitution, covering its preamble, general principles, citizens' rights and duties, the structure of state organs and national symbols. Useful as a primary source for how the state is organized.
readIf: You want the primary text of China's constitution for comparison or reference.
takeaway: Sets out the structure of the Chinese state and the rights and duties of citizens.

title: Constitution of France
about: The text of the French constitution of the Fifth Republic, covering sovereignty, the President, the Government, Parliament, the judiciary and the Constitutional Council. It defines the semi-presidential system.
readIf: You want the primary text of the French constitution for comparison or reference.
takeaway: Establishes France's Fifth Republic and its balance of power between president, government and parliament.

title: Basic Law for the Federal Republic of Germany
about: Germany's constitution, called the Basic Law. It opens with fundamental rights, then sets out the federal structure, the Bundestag, Bundesrat, President, Chancellor, and the Federal Constitutional Court.
readIf: You want the primary text of Germany's constitution for comparison or reference.
takeaway: Puts human dignity and basic rights first and builds a federal parliamentary system around them.

title: Constitution of India
about: The text of India's constitution, one of the longest in the world. It covers the preamble, fundamental rights, directive principles, the Union and states, Parliament, the judiciary, emergency provisions and amendment procedure, plus schedules.
readIf: You want the primary text of India's constitution for study or reference.
takeaway: Sets up a federal parliamentary republic with guaranteed fundamental rights and directive principles.

title: Constitution of Japan
about: The post-war constitution of Japan. It defines the Emperor as a symbol of the state, renounces war in Article 9, lists the rights and duties of the people, and sets out the Diet, Cabinet, judiciary and local government. It is relatively short.
readIf: You want the primary text of Japan's constitution, including the war-renouncing Article 9.
takeaway: Establishes popular sovereignty, a symbolic emperor and the renunciation of war.

title: Constitution of Russia
about: The text of the Russian Federation's constitution. It covers the foundations of the constitutional system, rights and freedoms, the federal structure, the President, the Federal Assembly, the Government and the judiciary.
readIf: You want the primary text of Russia's constitution for comparison or reference.
takeaway: Defines Russia as a federal state with a strong presidency.

title: Constitution of the United States
about: The US Constitution, covering the separation of powers among Congress, the President and the courts, federalism, and the amendment process. It also includes the amendments, with the Bill of Rights as the first ten.
readIf: You want the primary text of the US Constitution and its amendments.
takeaway: Creates a federal republic with checks and balances and a list of protected individual rights.

title: English Grammar in Use (5th edition)
authors: Raymond Murphy
about: A self-study grammar reference and practice book for intermediate learners of English. Each unit explains a point on one page, such as tenses, modals, articles or prepositions, with exercises on the facing page and an answer key at the back.
readIf: You are an intermediate English learner who wants short explanations followed by exercises.
takeaway: Learn one grammar point at a time through a short explanation and immediate practice.
